questions.prompt: How does abandoned memory differ from an isolated retain cycle?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: Abandoned memory is automatically cleared during low memory warnings.
options.explanation: ARC cannot clear abandoned memory unless your code removes strong references.

options.text: Retain cycles are allocated on the stack rather than on the heap.
options.explanation: Both retain cycles and abandoned objects reside in heap memory.

options.text: Abandoned memory crashes immediately when a view controller closes.
options.explanation: Abandoned memory lingers silently on the heap without triggering crashes.

options.text: Abandoned memory remains reachable from a root object such as a cache.
options.explanation: Abandoned memory is still reachable through roots, so ARC cannot deallocate it.

questions.prompt: What is the primary trade-off when selecting All Allocations and History for Malloc Stack Logging?

options.text: It completely disables breakpoint debugging and LLDB console commands.
options.explanation: LLDB breakpoints and console commands continue functioning normally.

options.text: It consumes extra memory and storage tracking historical allocations.
options.explanation: Logging all historical allocation call stacks introduces runtime memory overhead.

options.text: It forces ARC to use garbage collection instead of reference counting.
options.explanation: Swift uses ARC on all Apple platforms; it does not switch to garbage collection.

options.text: It prevents the app from opening network connections to secure hosts.

questions.prompt: Why is dirty memory particularly dangerous on iOS devices?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: Dirty memory causes Swift compiler warnings during automated builds.
options.explanation: Dirty memory is a runtime memory condition, not a compiler build warning.

options.text: Dirty memory prevents unit tests from executing in debug schemes.
options.explanation: Unit tests run independently of whether memory regions are dirty.

options.text: Dirty memory is discarded immediately without warning by the kernel.
options.explanation: iOS cannot discard dirty memory because it contains written data with no backing store.

options.text: iOS lacks swap space, so excessive dirty memory triggers Jetsam kills.
options.explanation: Because iOS has no disk swap, the operating system terminates apps using too much dirty memory.

questions.prompt: How do you break a strong reference cycle between a view controller and a stored closure?

options.text: Add a weak or unowned capture list such as [weak self] inside the closure.
options.explanation: A weak capture list ensures the closure does not increase the reference count of self.

options.text: Change the view controller class declaration into a value type struct.
options.explanation: View controllers inherit from UIViewController and must remain reference type classes.

options.text: Mark the closure property with the lazy modifier inside the class.
options.explanation: Lazy properties do not prevent closures from creating strong retain cycles.

options.text: Wrap the closure call inside an autoreleasepool block at runtime.
options.explanation: Autorelease pools manage temporary Objective-C objects, not Swift strong cycles.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how the Xcode Memory Graph debugger detects retain cycles compared to abandoned memory. Describe what visual indicator Xcode uses for retain cycles.

rubric.criterion: Explains that retain cycles form isolated islands of mutually strong references without external roots
Identifies the purple exclamation badge as the visual indicator for retain cycles
Explains that abandoned memory remains attached to a root object such as a singleton or collection

questions.modelAnswer: The Xcode Memory Graph debugger pauses the app and scans heap allocations for circular reference paths. When objects strongly reference each other with no remaining root pointers, Xcode marks them with a purple exclamation badge. In contrast, abandoned memory stays reachable through an active root object. Because of this root reference, Xcode shows no purple badge.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain Malloc Stack Logging. State where to enable it, and explain why it helps find leaks.

rubric.criterion: States where to enable Malloc Stack Logging (Scheme Diagnostics tab under Run action)
Explains that it records the full allocation backtrace or call stack for heap allocations
Explains that selecting a node in the Memory Graph reveals the exact file and line that created it

questions.modelAnswer: Malloc Stack Logging is enabled in the scheme diagnostics tab under the Run action. It records the full call stack for every memory allocation on the heap. When enabled, selecting an object in the Memory Graph debugger displays the exact file and line number that created that instance. Without it, you can only see that an object exists, but not where it came from.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, describe why a dismissed screen might leak without a purple badge. Explain how you locate it in the Memory Graph.

rubric.criterion: Describes a valid scenario such as registering with NotificationCenter or appending to a singleton manager
Explains why the purple badge is missing (the instance is still reachable from a root)
Explains how to locate it (filtering by class name in the navigator and checking instance count)

questions.modelAnswer: A dismissed view controller will leak without a purple badge if a long-lived singleton or notification observer retains it. Because the singleton is a root object, the view controller is still reachable, so Xcode does not flag it as an isolated cycle. To locate this leak, I filter the Debug Navigator by class name. Then I check if the instance count stays above zero after dismissal.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how a team automates memory leak checks in CI/CD. Mention memory graphs and command-line tools.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Mentions generating or exporting a .memgraph file from tests or command line
Mentions running the leaks or malloc_history command-line tool on the memgraph
Explains failing the automated build if leaks reports retain cycles

questions.modelAnswer: Teams can export a .memgraph snapshot during UI or integration tests using terminal commands or test attachments. In continuous integration, a shell step runs the leaks command-line utility against the exported memgraph file. If leaks identifies retain cycles or abandoned allocations, it exits with a non-zero status code, failing the build automatically before code merges.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain the difference between weak and unowned references when resolving retain cycles. When should you avoid unowned?

rubric.criterion: Explains that weak becomes nil when the target deallocates and is always an optional
Explains that unowned assumes the target is never nil and crashes if accessed after deallocation
States to avoid unowned when lifetimes are asynchronous, independent, or uncertain

questions.modelAnswer: A weak reference does not keep the target alive and becomes nil automatically when the instance deallocates, requiring an optional type. An unowned reference also avoids incrementing reference count, but assumes the target remains alive throughout its access. You should avoid unowned in asynchronous callbacks or network closures where the target might deallocate before the block executes, which would cause a crash.
